top.name: Reasoning effort xhigh -> medium, set where it takes effect (--default-reasoning-effort or chat_template_kwargs.reasoning_effort)
top.expected_gain: +13-24% agent wall time (reasoning = 53% of agent time; 25-45% token cut assumed)
top.why: Largest lever in the study. dsh's reasoning setting never reaches Splash (pi-ai sends no reasoning_effort, openai-completions.js:654-658), so the template defaults to xhigh with a 'consider alternatives' instruction (qwen38_gguf.jinja:58-69).
top.first_experiment: No GPU: render the template with effort unset vs medium to confirm the diff. Then GPU eval: t1/t2/t3 x3 reps, medium vs xhigh, comparing wall_s, output tokens and hidden_passed. Kill on a pass-rate drop or a reasoning-token cut under 15%.

top.name: Copy branches past depth 7 inside the 16-node best-first heap (Phase A: host root copy chain aligned with DFlash nodes)
top.expected_gain: +9.0% tokens/cycle simulated at T=0 (4.449->4.850), about +8.5% decode, about +5% agent; Phase A +5.4% tokens/cycle
top.exact: exact (rows independent of siblings; confirm by greedy digest)
top.why: The depth-7 cap binds in 20% of T=0 agent cycles and 49% of T=0.6 code cycles. The result is simulated within the 16-row budget, not guessed. Plumbing includes the 8-row DFlashDraft::addContextCommit (DFlashDraft.cpp:327-328), the accept caps (sampling.metal:1662, Runtime.mm:1889) and 8 more uniforms.
top.first_experiment: One GPU run: a T=0.6 SPLASH_DRAFT_DUMP over 20-50 dsh steps. Then offline sim.py/aligned.py to tune c and n. Kill below +3% at T=0.6. The same dump also feeds E4's threshold and the tau_tree check.

top.name: Re-tune staged K splits for one-lane decode (split-policy tier plus per-format overrides)
top.expected_gain: -0.66 ms already measured, -1 to -2.5 ms per cycle with per-format tiers: +1-3% decode, +0.6-1.8% agent
top.why: It was rejected only for its B4 cost, and decode is now capped at one lane. kernel-ab-diag shows 7-10% faster splits for down projections and QKV (ops/LinearGguf.cpp:81 kStagedTiers).
top.first_experiment: GPU, minutes: gguf-projection-benchmark split sweep for all verify shapes at L1, then a decode-profile A-B-B-A. Kill if the gain is under 0.5 ms per cycle.

top.name: Runaway-reasoning guard (force Qwen's </think> early-stop sequence at about 10-12K reasoning tokens, or stop on line repetition)
top.expected_gain: +4-8% agent time on sessions where it fires (4 cap steps = 11.4% of corpus agent time, with no output)
top.why: This is the worst single waste in the session logs, and steps below the budget are untouched.
top.first_experiment: No GPU: replay the 4 runaway transcripts and all normal reasoning blocks through a repetition detector to choose B and count false positives. GPU only to check that the forced close yields a valid tool call.

top.name: Cut IQ dequant instructions: E3 lean bit-identical grid decode (magic-number bytes, sign folded into the fp32 scale, sign index decoded once per group), then E5 integer-operand stage with a per-superblock scale chain
top.expected_gain: E3: 4-5 ms per cycle, +5-6% decode. E5: 5-8 ms, +6-10% decode, ceiling 8-9 ms (Q4_K-level dequant on 48 ms of grid-format projections). About +3-6% agent
top.why: Dequant and MMA costs add (kernel-ab-diag: 0.2254 = 0.113 matmul + 0.093 dequant + loads), so only fewer ALU ops per weight pay. Grid decode is about 9-11 ops per weight vs Q4_K's about 4-5. The matmul half already runs at the matrix-unit FP16 peak (25 TFLOP/s).
top.first_experiment: GPU microbenchmark: implement E3 for IQ3_S/IQ3_XXS in a dev copy, check bitwise stage equality, and time gguf-projection-benchmark 17408x5120. Kill E3 if IQ3_XXS is not under 0.21 ms (now 0.225). Then prototype E5 on IQ3_S; kill if not under 0.19 ms or if the fp64 test fails.

top.name: Per-cycle verify row count: skip the second 8-row attention tile at long context when nodes 8-15 are improbable
top.expected_gain: Gated simulation: +2.4% at 64K, +5.4% at 96K, +8.9% at 128K; about +3-4% decode over long sessions, about +2% agent
top.exact: exact (smaller tree, same accept rule; confirm by digest)
top.why: Real sessions run at 30-120K context, where 25-45 ms per cycle is context-dependent attention. It is the only exact idea aimed there; the 16 and 8x2 tiles lost.
top.first_experiment: GPU: decode-profile at 32K/64K/96K with the second tile forced to early-exit. Kill if 64K does not drop by at least 5 ms from 114.8. Then set theta(L) with gate.py on the T=0.6 dump.

top.name: Finish the park lane (oracle test, then ship under the exact-math rule if it is a near-tie)
top.expected_gain: +3.5% agent time (own-output re-prefill = 38-44% of per-step prefill tokens; measured prompt time -24% over 6 turns)
top.exact: approximate (pending oracle; exact-math if a near-tie)
top.why: The code is done and adoption works (4/5, 0 mismatches). It is blocked only on deciding whether the char-127 divergence is a near-tie.
top.first_experiment: GPU: same prompt, park->adopt vs cold prefill; dump the logits at the first differing token. A top-2 margin under about 0.05 means a near-tie.

top.name: Matrix-unit probes: int8 / half x int8 / e4m3 matmul2d rate, relaxed_precision=true, and MMA-vs-ALU concurrency (gates W8A8, int8-B stage and producer/consumer specialization)
top.expected_gain: If INT8 runs at about 2x FP16 at 16 rows: W8A8 gives +35-40% decode (approximate); int8-B stage about +10%; specialization up to +30% if MMA and ALU overlap. Low prior (0.15-0.25)
top.exact: probe itself n/a; W8A8 approximate, int8-B exact-math, specialization exact
top.why: This is the only path past the FP16 matrix-unit floor of about 34 ms. External data (tzakharko INT8 about 2x per core; Draw Things fused int8 1.61-1.87x on M5) makes it worth one day. MLX uses relaxed_precision=true; Splash uses false.
top.first_experiment: GPU microbenchmark, 1 day: time a nodeq-style 16x32x32 matmul2d with half, int8 and e4m3 operands, with and without relaxed_precision, plus a concurrent dispatch of matmul-only and dequant-only kernels (max vs sum). Kill W8A8 if int8 is under 1.3x half; kill specialization if the concurrent time is about the sum.

ranked.summary:
I merged the five reports into /Users/abdul.rakib/agentMania/dsh-qwen-jev/splash/RESEARCH-ADVANCED-2026-11-02.md. It replaces the old copy, which was byte-identical to the backup RESEARCH-ADVANCED-2026-11-02.run1.md. Nothing ran on the GPU.

**Two corrections to the time budget:**
- The GPU idles about 0.63 ms between cycles, not 2-3 ms. Angle 2 measured this over about 15,000 cycles.
- Angle 1's estimate of 12-16 ms saved by a faster IQ dequant was too high. It assumed IQ formats are 90% of verify time; IQ3/IQ2 are 72% of verify bytes, and IQ4_XS is not a grid format. Taking their dequant to Q4_K's measured cost saves at most 8-9 ms per cycle, about +10% decode.

**What is still movable inside a cycle:** the matmul half of each projection already runs at the M5 matrix units' FP16 peak (2.85 GFLOP in 0.113 ms = 25 TFLOP/s). So the 41 ms bandwidth floor is not reachable this way. What can still shrink is about 19-23 ms of dequant, plus a possible int8 matmul rate that nobody has measured on this chip.

**At the agent level, reasoning tokens matter most.** They are 53% of agent time, and the template runs at xhigh effort because dsh's reasoning setting never reaches Splash.

**Ranking:**
1. Reasoning effort xhigh to medium: about +13-24% agent time, but approximate, so it needs the eval.
2. Copy branches past depth 7 inside the 16-node tree: +9% tokens/cycle in angle 3's simulation, about +5% agent time, exact.
3. Re-tune the K splits now that decode runs one lane: +1-3% decode.
4. Runaway-reasoning guard: removes the steps that hit 16K tokens and returned nothing.
5. Cut instructions in the IQ dequant: a bit-identical lean decode first, then integer staging with the scale applied once per 256-weight superblock (+5-10% decode).
6. Skip the second 8-row attention tile per cycle at long context.
7. Finish the park lane, which is blocked on one oracle test.
8. A one-day microbenchmark of int8 matmul rates, `relaxed_precision` and matmul/dequant overlap, which decides three high-variance kernel ideas.

**Rejected or deferred:** pre-encoding the next cycle and indirect command buffers (capped at the 0.63 ms gap), folding the GDN commit into the next verify (net loss), folding norms into projections, llama.cpp's few-row simdgroup MMA (slower on M5), trees above 16 nodes or fixed tree shapes, multi-draft acceptance, and the asf0 block-16 drafter. The Weaver tree adapter is deferred: it needs about 15 days plus rented GPUs to generate training data.

**Open gap for the next round:** at the 30-120K contexts dsh actually runs, 25-45 ms of every cycle is context-dependent verify attention. Only the attention-tile skip (rank 6) touches it, and it deserves its own study.

The report also gives the cheapest first experiment for each top idea and marks which ones need the GPU.

skeptics.name: Re-tune staged K splits for one-lane decode (split-policy tier plus per-format overrides)
skeptics.realistic_gain: -0.6 to -1.1 ms per ~84 ms cycle: +0.7 to +1.3% decode tok/s, about +0.4 to +0.8% agent wall time. The claimed -1 to -2.5 ms (+1-3%) range is refuted. Its upper half is larger than an oracle that picks the best split for every shape. The direction is real, it is cheap (0.5-1 day), and it is worth doing as a small item. Kill threshold: about 0.5 ms, near the noise.
skeptics.flaws:
1. The upper bound is larger than the measured oracle. In the split sweep, weighted by the 27B's dispatches per step (logs/speed/round-20261021-0121/split-policy.txt:226-230), picking the fastest split for every (shape, format) saves only:
   - L1: 51.866 -> 50.497 ms, -1.37 ms;
   - L2: 49.199 -> 48.229 ms, -0.97 ms.
   No set of per-format tiers can beat that oracle. Those are isolated-kernel numbers, and they shrink once the kernels run in the real cycle (point 2), so -2.5 ms is not reachable and even -1 ms is optimistic.
2. Isolated savings shrink in the real cycle. The sweep predicted -0.95 ms at L1 for split-policy. The decode-profile measured -1.24 ms on top of upstream, but only -0.66 ms on top of m16 (84.63 -> 83.97). With B2 on m16 as a proxy for 16 rows, it measured -0.85 ms (88.94 -> 88.09, SPEED_LOG.md:325-330).
3. Per-format overrides add little. The extra headroom over split-policy is 0.3-0.4 ms isolated: L1 50.912 -> 50.497, L2 48.534 -> 48.229. That is about 0.2-0.3 ms in the real cycle. It mostly comes from undoing split-policy's own regressions:
   - IQ4_XS ffn-down +3.5-5.1%;
   - IQ4_XS gdn-qkv and gdn-z +4%.
   So the realistic total is -0.66 ms (measured) plus 0.1-0.3 ms, i.e. -0.7 to -1.1 ms.
4. Not all the evidence matches today's tile and tree. The split-check and kernel-ab-diag tables were measured on the 32-row tile, before m16. All the evidence comes from before the 16-node tree:
   - stagedComputeRows (LinearGguf.cpp:30) computes 16 rows either way, so the 16-row compute pattern carries over.
   - The 32-row-tile optimum for each format may still shift on the m16 tile.
   - The "7-10% faster" figures (SPEED_PLAN.md:77) were flagged there as a single run that needs confirming.
5. The logs already describe these gains as noise-sized. The B4 +0.8% was called run-to-run noise (SPEED_LOG.md:344). A gain of 0.6-1.1 ms (0.7-1.3%) is barely above that and needs a careful A-B-B-A to resolve. The proposed 0.5 ms kill threshold is about the noise floor.
6. Plumbing is more than a table edit. decodeSplits(n,k,cores,tiers) (LinearGguf.cpp:49-57) sees only the shape, not the format. Per-format overrides must pass the segment format into stagedDecode. Fused multi-format plans also need a rule: attn-input-fused q2k+iq3s+q4k is 11.7% off its best split (split-policy.txt:215-216). That tips the effort toward 1 day, not 0.75.
7. Exactness:
   - The math is exact, but fp32 partial sums are added in a different order, so the result is not bit-identical to today. Greedy text can diverge from today's at near-ties.
   - Output stays deterministic and independent of batching, because splits depend only on (n, k, format), not on rows or lanes.
   - The m16 bar of 12 bit-identical greedy answers will not hold. Validation needs the gguf-projection fp64 test plus an accuracy spot check instead.
8. No hidden memory or occupancy cost was found. More splits only add partial-sum scratch and a reduce step, which is already counted in the benchmark times.
